stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okafor's conclusion?
stimulus:
Most printed maps put north at the top. Many digital navigation apps instead rotate the map so that the direction the traveler is facing is always up. Cartographer Lena Okafor and her colleagues asked volunteers to walk unfamiliar routes with one of the two map styles and counted their wrong turns. The volunteers were grouped by whether they had any prior orienteering experience. Okafor concluded that turning the map to match the traveler's heading reduces navigation errors among novice map readers.

Average Wrong Turns per Route
Map reader | North-up map | Heading-up map
Novice | 4.2 | 1.8
Experienced | 1.1 | 1.0
choices: Experienced readers averaged 1.1 wrong turns with north-up maps and 1.0 wrong turns with heading-up maps.
Novice readers averaged 4.2 wrong turns with north-up maps and 1.8 wrong turns with heading-up maps.
Novice readers averaged 4.2 wrong turns with north-up maps, while experienced readers averaged 1.1 wrong turns.
Novice readers averaged 1.8 wrong turns with north-up maps and 4.2 wrong turns with heading-up maps.
explanation: Okafor's conclusion is about one group, novice readers, and one comparison: heading-up maps versus north-up maps. To support it, you need novice readers to make fewer wrong turns with heading-up maps. Choice B shows exactly that: 1.8 wrong turns compared with 4.2.

A.why: These numbers are accurate, but they describe experienced readers. The conclusion is limited to novices, so you compared the right map styles for the wrong group.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares novices with experienced readers who were both using north-up maps. The conclusion is about the effect of map style, and this choice never compares the two styles.

D.why: You swapped the columns. In the table, novices averaged 4.2 wrong turns with north-up maps, not with heading-up maps. Read this way, the data would weaken the conclusion.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the planners' hypothesis?
stimulus:
A city transportation office studied 12 pairs of streets. The two streets in each pair had similar traffic, width and nearby housing. One street in each pair had a bike lane marked only with paint. The other had a lane separated from cars by a raised curb. The office counted cyclists on both streets for six months. Because commuters tend to avoid riding next to heavy rush-hour traffic, the planners hypothesized that curb-separated lanes draw more cyclists than painted lanes on weekdays.

Average Daily Cyclists per Street
Lane type | Weekdays | Weekends
Painted lane | 310 | 420
Curb-separated lane | 680 | 450
choices: On weekends, streets with curb-separated lanes averaged 450 cyclists, and streets with painted lanes averaged 420.
Streets with painted lanes averaged 420 cyclists on weekends but only 310 cyclists on weekdays.
On weekdays, streets with curb-separated lanes averaged 680 cyclists, and streets with painted lanes averaged 310.
On weekdays, streets with painted lanes averaged 680 cyclists, and streets with curb-separated lanes averaged 310.
explanation: The hypothesis applies only to weekdays and compares the two lane types. To support it, the curb-separated lanes need more weekday cyclists than the painted lanes. Choice C reports that comparison: 680 cyclists versus 310.

A.why: The numbers are right, but they come from the weekend column. The hypothesis is limited to weekdays, so this choice skips the condition the claim depends on.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares days of the week for one lane type. The hypothesis needs a comparison between the two lane types, and this choice never makes one.

D.why: You attached the weekday numbers to the wrong lane types. The table gives 680 for curb-separated lanes and 310 for painted lanes. Read this way, the data would weaken the hypothesis.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Reyes's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Fresh snow reflects most incoming sunlight and gives off heat efficiently into a clear night sky, so the ground under it cools quickly after sunset. The chilled surface then cools the layer of air just above it. Meteorologist Tomás Reyes compared overnight low temperatures at weather stations on a valley floor and on a nearby ridge. He sorted nights with snow on the ground from nights without it. Reyes hypothesizes that snow cover produces much colder nights at valley-floor stations.

Average Overnight Low (°C)
Station location | Snow-covered nights | Bare-ground nights
Valley floor | −14 | −7
Ridge top | −9 | −8
choices: At valley-floor stations, the average low was −14°C on snow-covered nights and −7°C on bare-ground nights.
At ridge-top stations, the average low was −9°C on snow-covered nights and −8°C on bare-ground nights.
On snow-covered nights, the average low was −14°C at valley-floor stations and −9°C at ridge-top stations.
At valley-floor stations, the average low was −7°C on snow-covered nights and −14°C on bare-ground nights.
explanation: The hypothesis is about valley-floor stations, and it compares nights with snow to nights without it. Choice A stays on the valley floor and shows that snow-covered nights were much colder: −14°C compared with −7°C.

B.why: The numbers are accurate, but they come from the ridge-top row. The hypothesis is limited to valley-floor stations, so this is the right comparison in the wrong place.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares the two locations on snowy nights. The hypothesis is about whether snow makes valley nights colder, so you need snow and bare ground at the same location.

D.why: You reversed the valley-floor values. In the table, the −14°C low goes with snow-covered nights, not bare-ground nights.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nandakumar's conclusion?
stimulus:
Madder root produces a red dye that does not bond well to fibers by itself. Dyers in medieval Europe often soaked cloth in alum first. Alum is a mineral salt that binds to both the fiber and the dye. Textile historian Priya Nandakumar re-created this process. She dyed samples of wool and linen with madder, some with alum and some without, and then washed each sample twenty times. She concludes that alum was essential to the long-lasting reds of medieval woolens.

Color Retained After 20 Washes (%)
Fiber | With alum | Without alum
Wool | 85 | 40
Linen | 45 | 30
choices: Linen samples dyed with alum retained 45% of their color, and those dyed without alum retained 30%.
Wool and linen samples dyed with alum retained 85% and 45% of their color, respectively.
Wool samples dyed with alum retained 40% of their color, and those dyed without alum retained 85%.
Wool samples dyed with alum retained 85% of their color, and those dyed without alum retained 40%.
explanation: The conclusion is about woolens, and it says alum made the difference. To support it, you need wool dyed with alum compared with wool dyed without alum. Choice D shows wool keeping 85% of its color with alum and only 40% without it.

A.why: These figures are accurate, but they describe linen. The conclusion is about woolens, so you made the right comparison for the wrong fabric.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares two fabrics that were both treated with alum. To show that alum was essential, you have to compare samples with alum to samples without it.

C.why: You swapped the wool columns. In the table, the wool dyed with alum is the sample that retained 85% of its color.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Sato's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Spiral galaxies have lanes of dust concentrated in their flat disks. When we see a galaxy edge-on, starlight has to pass through much more of that dust than when we see the galaxy face-on. Dust absorbs visible light far more strongly than infrared light. For that reason, astronomer Hana Sato expected a galaxy's orientation to matter mainly for one kind of measurement. She hypothesizes that edge-on spirals appear substantially dimmer than face-on spirals in visible light.

Average Surface Brightness of Spiral Galaxies (relative units)
Orientation | Visible light | Infrared light
Face-on | 80 | 60
Edge-on | 35 | 58
choices: In infrared light, edge-on spirals had an average brightness of 58 units, and face-on spirals had an average of 60.
Face-on spirals had an average brightness of 80 units in visible light and 60 units in infrared light.
In visible light, edge-on spirals had an average brightness of 35 units, and face-on spirals had an average of 80.
In visible light, edge-on spirals had an average brightness of 80 units, and face-on spirals had an average of 35.
explanation: The hypothesis is limited to visible light, and it says edge-on spirals should look dimmer than face-on spirals. Choice C uses the visible-light column and shows that edge-on galaxies were much dimmer: 35 units compared with 80.

A.why: These values are accurate, but they come from the infrared column. The hypothesis covers visible light only, so this choice skips the condition the claim depends on.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares two kinds of light for face-on galaxies only. The hypothesis is about how edge-on and face-on galaxies differ, and this choice never compares them.

D.why: You assigned the visible-light values to the wrong orientations. The table gives 35 units for edge-on spirals and 80 for face-on spirals.
